title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
summary: While the industry cites "uncertainty" in future fuels, two-thirds of the global fleet is projected to avoid major retrofits, ensuring prolonged reliance on conventional, high-carbon fuels. The proposed "layered strategy" for the majority non-retrofitted vessels, seeking "measurable emissions reductions today" without capital, risks merely delaying substantial FuelEU Maritime fines if it doesn't drastically improve carbon intensity. Real R&D and lifecycle support must deliver immediate, tangible carbon reductions for the existing fleet, not just future fuel complexity, otherwise many ships will continue to exceed their CII ratings and incur penalties.
content:
Ship owners are at a crossroads. They are being asked to make long-term capital commitments in conditions of genuine uncertainty. Many of the fuels needed to comply with environmental regulations in the long term are not available at the scale needed. The infrastructure to support them is still being built, as well as a lack of clarity and investment on where the fuels will come from. On top of this, the regulatory frameworks that will ultimately determine how shipping decarbonises are still being debated. Against that backdrop of operational limbo, the question that matters most is how ship owners can actually continue to grow and not get left behind.

Industry analysis suggests that roughly two-thirds of the existing global fleet will not undergo major retrofits for next-generation fuels, primarily because of vessel age and the economics involved. For this majority, the industry needs solutions that deliver measurable emissions reductions today, without introducing operational risk or requiring capital commitments that cannot be justified.

One approach to this challenge is in adopting a layered strategy, one that matches the right solution to the right vessel, at the right point in its lifecycle. Fuel supply systems are an enabler of that strategy, and the confidence to invest in them depends, more than anything else, on the quality of the engineering, R&D and lifecycle support that underpins them.

Complexity demands preparation

The transition away from conventional marine fuels is not simply a question of swapping one product for another. Alternative fuels introduce genuine technical complexity that must be resolved before it reaches the vessel.

Methanol requires specific safety system configurations – gas detection, leak detection and emergency shutdown capability – as well as crew training that goes well beyond conventional fuel oil handling. Ammonia presents greater challenges, from additional tank configurations, isolation from crew accommodation and heat sources, specialised safety measures and extensive operational training.

Even biofuels, often positioned as the most straightforward near-term option, require careful thought around viscosity, cold flow properties and compatibility with existing onboard equipment. None of these challenges are insurmountable, but they require investment in research, testing and real-world operating experience before they can be managed with confidence.

Documented, applied research into how alternative fuels behave in practice, and how fuel supply systems must be designed to handle them, is the foundation on which ship owner confidence is built. When a supplier can demonstrate through rigorous testing that their equipment has been designed and validated accordingly, the decision for ship owners to invest in alternative fuels becomes substantially easier.

The near-term case for biofuels

Within a layered strategy, higher-flashpoint biofuels have a strong near-term role. SOLAS Chapter II-2 compliant fuels such as HVO and FAME can often function as drop-in replacements, requiring minimal modification to existing engines and fuel supply systems, no alternative design approvals and, in most cases, no dry docking.

Furthermore, under EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, vessels calling at European ports face direct financial exposure based on their greenhouse gas intensity. For operators managing mixed fleets with varied compliance timelines, biofuels offer a credible bridge: reducing emissions today, at a fraction of the cost of full alternative-fuel conversion.

Short-sea, feeder and regional vessels with frequent European port calls are among the earliest movers. Tanker, ro-ro and ro-pax fleets with centralised fleet management are following. In the newbuild space, methanol dual-fuel is gaining strong momentum in the container feeder and chemical tanker segments, where the economics of a longer asset life make the investment case more straightforward. Older ships are typically best served by low-capital biofuel blends and mid-life vessels can often justify moderate fuel supply system upgrades. The fuel supply system connects these layers and determines which fuels can be used, how safely and efficiently they are handled, and what the vessel’s real-world emissions profile actually looks like.

The reality is that fuel specifications evolve, regulatory requirements change and operational profiles shift as vessels move between trade routes. This is why lifecycle services are integral to the value of any decarbonisation investment, not an optional extra. Lifecycle support encompasses commissioning, scheduled service inspections, maintenance, predictive spare parts management, upgrades, crew training and remote monitoring. Together, these ensure the fuel supply system continues to perform efficiently across the vessel’s operational life, and that when fuel specifications or regulations change, the system can keep up.
